# How to Spot a Deepfake Video or Voice Clone Before You Share It

> **In short:** Look closely at the video and listen to the voice for oddities, read what the clip asks you to do, and check with the real person through a number or channel you already trust. If anything feels off, don't forward it, and never send money, gift cards or crypto because of a clip or a call.

A short clip of a public figure saying something outrageous lands in your family group chat. A frantic voicemail from your "boss" asks you to buy gift cards. Neither is obviously fake, and that's exactly the point. A **deepfake** is a video, image or audio clip made with AI to look or sound like a real person who never actually said or did the thing, and **voice cloning** means reproducing someone's voice from recordings of them speaking. The FBI warns that criminals use AI-generated audio and video to impersonate relatives, company executives and public figures in order to get money or access to accounts. Careful looking and listening can sometimes catch a fake, but no single check is perfect, so your final safety net is always verifying with the real person before you act or share.

## Before you start
- The clip itself (saved to your phone or laptop, or a link in a message)
- A way to reach the person it claims to come from, using a number or channel you already had
- About 2–3 minutes per clip
- No account, no app, no paid plan needed

## Step 1 — Look closely for flaws
Pause the video and study it for about 10 seconds, zooming in if you can. The FBI lists these possible flaws in AI-generated images and video: distorted hands or feet, odd-looking teeth or eyes, inaccurate shadows, watermarks, lag and unnatural movement. Compare the face, the hands and the lighting with the rest of the scene. A clip with none of these flaws can still be fake, so treat this as one clue, not a verdict. You'll know it worked when you've either spotted something that feels off or can say the clip looks natural — and you move on to the other checks either way.

## Step 2 — Listen to tone and word choice
Close your eyes for a moment and just listen. The FBI advises listening closely to tone and word choice to spot a cloned voice. Does it sound like the person you know? Would they really say it that way? Does the emotion fit the situation — for example, someone who is supposedly panicking but sounds calm and even? Keep in mind that a voice that sounds just like someone you know is not proof it's them, because criminals can fake a loved one's voice from short audio clips. You'll know it worked when you can say whether the voice and the wording fit the person — and you remember that a familiar voice still needs checking.

## Step 3 — Read what the message asks you to do
Before you forward anything or reply, stop and read the context. Who sent it? Is it really them, or just a forwarded link from someone you trust? What does the clip ask you to do — send money, click a link, share a code, keep quiet about something? The FTC lists four common signs of a scam: someone pretending to be from an organization you know, a problem or a prize, pressure to act right now, and demands that you pay in a specific way, such as with gift cards, cryptocurrency, a wire transfer or a payment app. The FTC adds that anyone who insists you can only pay that way is a scammer. Secrecy and big emotional claims ("don't tell anyone", "this is huge") are also good reasons to slow down. You'll know it worked when you have a clear answer to "who, what and why" — or a clear reason to be suspicious.

## Step 4 — Verify with the real person through a channel you trust
Contact the person or organization directly, using a number or channel you already had — not the one the clip or call came from. The FBI advises hanging up and contacting the organization directly using a number you find independently, and the FTC notes that scammers can fake caller ID, so a familiar name or number on the screen proves nothing. If you and your family have agreed on a secret word or phrase (the FBI suggests this), ask for it.
💬 Example: "Hey, I got a voice note from someone claiming to be you asking about gift cards. Did you actually send it? Just checking."
You'll know it worked when you have heard from the real person on a channel you trust, or decided the clip isn't worth the risk.

## Step 5 — Decide what to do next
If any of the checks above raised doubt, the safest move is simple: **don't share it** and don't send anything. Reposting a fake — even with a "this might be fake" caveat — still spreads the original. Tell the person who sent it, politely, that you couldn't verify it, and ask where they got it. If the clip claims to be someone you know, give them a heads-up that someone may be using their face or voice. The FBI advises against sending money, gift cards, cryptocurrency or other assets to people you know only online or by phone, and against sharing sensitive information with them. If you were targeted or lost money, contact your bank or the company being impersonated directly, and report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov (FTC) or ic3.gov (the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center). Outside the US, contact your local police or consumer protection agency. You can also report the clip to the platform where you saw it. You'll know it worked when you stop and think before tapping "forward."

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the "share if you agree" framing.** If a clip is trying to get you to forward it before you've checked, that's the scam working. Slow down — the share button can wait 30 seconds.
- **Assuming a familiar name or voice means it's really them.** Senders and caller IDs can be **spoofed** (a message or call made to look like it came from someone you know) and voices can be cloned. Verify through a separate channel before trusting.
- **Relying on a single check.** No single check — your own eyes and ears, or an "AI detection" tool — is reliable enough to be your only one. Combine them, and finish by verifying with the real person.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Treat any unexpected video or voice message that asks for money, codes or secrecy as suspicious until you've verified it through a channel you trust. The FBI also suggests agreeing on a secret word or phrase with family members, and limiting how much of your photos and voice you share publicly (for example, by setting social media accounts to private and accepting followers only if you know them).
- **For your work:** If a "colleague" sends an unusual request by voice or video, especially one involving wire transfers or credentials, confirm it through a known channel — a call to a number you already have, or a conversation in person — before acting.
- **If you're just getting started:** Save this page and use it as a checklist the next time a clip makes you feel strongly, good or bad. Strong feelings are exactly what fake clips are designed to trigger.

## Try it now
Agree on a secret word or phrase with your family this week, so you have a quick way to verify each other if a suspicious call or voice message ever arrives. Then pick one short video you saw recently that made you feel a strong reaction and spend two minutes running Steps 1 to 3 on it. Even if it turns out to be real, the practice makes the next check faster and easier.
